case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a crime qualifies as an INA aggravated felony "offense relating to obstruction of justice" even if it does not require a nexus to a pending or ongoing investigation or judicial proceeding.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(S) (defining as an aggravated felony "an offense relating to obstruction of justice").
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that "obstruction of justice" has a well-settled generic meaning requiring interference with an existing (pending or ongoing) investigation or judicial proceeding; because the Virginia accessory-after-the-fact offense can be committed without any such nexus, it falls outside § 1101(a)(43)(S). Petitioner also invokes the rule of lenity in immigration/removal contexts (interpreting ambiguity in the narrowest way given deportation’s severe consequences).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General argues that § 1101(a)(43)(S) covers offenses "relating to" obstruction of justice broadly, including conduct that intentionally impedes the process of justice even when no investigation or proceeding is yet pending; thus accessory-after-the-fact (and similar crimes) can qualify as obstruction-related aggravated felonies without a pending-proceeding nexus.
key_precedents: Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6 (1948)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s Aguilar-based “term of art” argument is the hardest point for the Petitioner because it plausibly identifies a proceeding-nexus feature in some federal obstruction statutes circa 1996. But Aguilar construed §1503’s omnibus clause, not the INA’s aggravated-felony category, and Congress’s choice of “an offense relating to obstruction of justice” (as Justice Thomas stresses via Morales) is difficult to square with importing §1503’s specific nexus as a categorical prerequisite across diverse state offenses. Justice Sotomayor’s Fong Haw Tan point properly cautions against overexpansion in removal, yet under ordinary textual tools the “relating to” modifier supplies enough breadth that we need not—and should not, as a minimalist matter—add an atextual pending-proceeding requirement to decide this accessory-after-the-fact–type case. I would affirm narrowly: an offense intentionally aimed at hindering apprehension or punishment can “relate to” obstruction without a formally pending proceeding, leaving outer-limit questions for future cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s Aguilar-based “term of art” argument is the strongest for petitioner, but it overreads Aguilar as fixing a generic 1996 meaning for the INA. Aguilar construed §1503’s omnibus clause in its particular statutory setting; it did not purport to define the original public meaning of Congress’s different phrase—an offense “relating to obstruction of justice”—and, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, “relating to” is an enacted broadener that we cannot treat as surplusage by importing a rigid pending-proceeding nexus as a categorical prerequisite. Justice Sotomayor’s Fong Haw Tan point does not alter the analysis because, under ordinary textual meaning (consistent with Morales’s treatment of “relating to”), the statute is not in genuine equipoise such that lenity can justify adding an atextual limitation. On an originalist and textualist approach, accessory-after-the-fact conduct intentionally aimed at hindering apprehension or punishment bears a sufficient relationship to obstruction of justice even absent a formally pending proceeding.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s Aguilar-based argument is the most serious: that “obstruction of justice” in 1996 often carried a pending-proceeding nexus, and “relating to” merely captures variants of that core. But Aguilar construed the elements of §1503’s omnibus clause; it did not purport to define the INA’s aggravated-felony category, and Congress’s deliberate addition of “relating to” (as Justice Thomas and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, consistent with Morales’s broad connective reading) signals a wider sweep than importing §1503’s nexus as a categorical prerequisite. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Fong Haw Tan is a legitimate caution given removal’s consequences, but under ordinary textual tools the enacted phrase is not genuinely in equipoise, and narrowing it to require a pending proceeding would undercut Congress’s evident law-enforcement-focused design to reach intentional assistance that hinders apprehension or punishment. I therefore remain with Respondent, while favoring a narrow holding that we need not define every outer limit beyond accessory-after-the-fact–type conduct aimed at thwarting justice.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s Morales-based emphasis on the breadth of “relating to” is the strongest point for Respondent, but it still assumes a meaningful anchor for “obstruction of justice” as a term of art in 1996; without that anchor, “relating to” risks turning §1101(a)(43)(S) into a sweeping post-offense-assistance catchall incompatible with the categorical approach. Justice Barrett is right to rely on Aguilar as evidence that the generic core of obstruction required a nexus to a proceeding (or at least an ongoing investigative/proceeding-like process), and “relating to” can expand to closely connected variants without deleting that core element. Morales arose in a preemption context and cannot do the work of severing a removal-triggering aggravated-felony category from its settled meaning, especially given the INA’s severe, mandatory consequences. Because the text-plus-backdrop leaves at least residual doubt about how far Congress meant to go, Fong Haw Tan’s narrow-construction principle properly counsels against the Respondent’s expansive reading urged by Justice Kagan and Justice Alito.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s term-of-art point (echoed by Justices Sotomayor and Jackson) is the hardest: “relating to” must have an anchor, and in 1996 many obstruction provisions were proceeding-linked. But Aguilar construed §1503’s omnibus clause, not the INA phrase Congress chose, and as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas stress, Congress added “relating to,” which under ordinary usage (and Morales’s connective reading) broadens the category beyond a rigid pending-proceeding nexus without making it limitless. The workable middle ground is to treat the generic core as intentional interference with the administration of justice—encompassing purposeful hindrance of apprehension or punishment—while reserving whether more attenuated, non-intentional, or regulatory offenses “relate to” obstruction for future cases. Because the text and structure give that much guidance, Fong Haw Tan does not justify importing Aguilar’s nexus as an across-the-board categorical element.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s Aguilar-based “term of art” point remains the best argument for Petitioner, because “relating to” cannot do all the definitional work if the anchor term had a fixed, proceeding-nexus core in 1996. But Aguilar construed §1503’s omnibus clause, not the INA’s aggravated-felony category, and—consistent with Justice Thomas’s reliance on Morales—the phrase Congress chose (“an offense relating to obstruction of justice”) is textually broader than importing §1503’s specific nexus element as a categorical prerequisite. I also agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower path: we can hold only that offenses intentionally aimed at hindering apprehension or punishment bear a sufficient relationship to obstruction even absent a formally pending proceeding, without turning §1101(a)(43)(S) into an unbounded catchall. Justice Sotomayor’s Fong Haw Tan caution is important, but it is a tie-breaker after ordinary tools; here, the enacted breadth of “relating to” supplies enough direction that lenity/narrow construction does not justify adding an atextual pending-proceeding requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s anchor-term argument, echoed by Justices Sotomayor and Jackson, is the hardest point: “relating to” cannot do all the definitional work, and Aguilar reflects a real proceeding-nexus theme in some federal obstruction provisions. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Aguilar construed §1503’s omnibus clause, not the INA’s aggravated-felony category, and Congress’s choice of the deliberately expansive phrase “an offense relating to obstruction of justice” (as in Morales) makes it methodologically unsound to import §1503’s nexus as a rigid categorical prerequisite across diverse state statutes. Fong Haw Tan’s narrow-construction principle in removal cases, highlighted by Justice Sotomayor, is a genuine caution, yet it is a tie-breaker only after ordinary textual tools leave true equipoise; here the enacted “relating to” language supplies enough clarity to cover purposeful interference with apprehension or punishment even before a formal proceeding. I therefore would affirm on the limited ground Roberts proposes, reserving outer-boundary questions to future cases to protect administrability and the Court’s legitimacy.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas press the strongest point for Respondent: Morales reads “relating to” broadly, and that breadth is hard to square with importing Aguilar’s §1503 nexus wholesale. But that modifier cannot do all the definitional work; it presupposes an anchored generic meaning for “obstruction of justice,” and in 1996 the ordinary legal meaning of that anchor in federal law and common usage was proceeding- (or at least investigation-) linked, so treating accessory-after-the-fact as categorically covered effectively rewrites the anchor to mean “hindering law enforcement” in general. Justice Kagan’s proposed middle ground (no pending proceeding required if the conduct aims to hinder apprehension or punishment) still detaches the category from the term of art Congress chose and risks collapsing §1101(a)(43)(S) into a broad post-offense assistance catchall, which is especially problematic under the categorical approach. Even if “relating to” expands coverage to close variants, Fong Haw Tan confirms that any residual uncertainty in a removal-triggering provision should be resolved narrowly rather than by allowing the modifier to swallow the anchored term.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest point for Respondent is Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s reliance on Morales to give “relating to” a broad sweep, but that still begs the threshold question Justice Barrett presses: what is the anchored generic meaning of “obstruction of justice” that the related-to clause presupposes. If we accept Roberts’s proposed rule—any intentional hindrance of apprehension or punishment qualifies—we effectively decouple the category from a proceeding- or proceeding/investigation-linked core and create an administrability and notice problem under the categorical approach, turning §1101(a)(43)(S) into a near-catchall aggravated-felony trigger. Justice Kagan’s middle-ground framing narrows the holding, but it still shifts the definition away from the term-of-art backdrop Congress legislated against in 1996 (Aguilar-era) and expands mandatory removal in ways that, under Fong Haw Tan’s caution in deportation statutes, we should not infer without clearer direction. On my pragmatic, fairness-centered view, the proceeding-linked nexus remains the best cabining principle that keeps “relating to” from swallowing the anchor and preserves predictable, elements-based adjudication.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) reaches “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and Congress’s use of “relating to” signals a broader sweep than a precise common-law or Title 18 label, allowing coverage of conduct intentionally aimed at thwarting the administration of justice even before a proceeding is formally pending. Reading the provision to require an ongoing or pending investigation/proceeding would narrow the text in a way that is difficult to reconcile with that expansive modifier and would unsettle the agency’s and several circuits’ longstanding treatment of accessory-after-the-fact–type offenses as obstruction-adjacent. While the petitioner invokes the immigration lenity principle from Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6 (1948), that canon applies only after exhausting ordinary tools of interpretation; here, the statutory phrase “relating to” provides a sufficient textual basis for a modest, institutionally cautious ruling affirming the Attorney General’s interpretation. The decision can be narrow: it need only hold that a categorical match does not require a pending-proceeding nexus where the offense involves intentional interference with the process of justice, leaving harder boundary cases for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text Congress enacted in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(S) does not define the aggravated felony as “obstruction of justice,” but as any “offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the ordinary public meaning of “relating to” at the time was broadly connective—covering offenses having a “connection with” the enumerated subject. Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc., 504 U.S. 374, 383–384 (1992), confirms that breadth, and nothing in the statutory text adds a pending-proceeding nexus requirement. Even if some federal obstruction statutes (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 1503) historically presupposed a proceeding, Congress’s choice to use the expansive “relating to” formulation in § 1101(a)(43)(S) indicates it meant to reach obstruction-type conduct beyond the tight common-law core, including intentional interference with the administration of justice before a proceeding is underway. Because the text is sufficiently clear, the rule of lenity invoked in Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6 (1948), does not justify importing an extra-textual nexus requirement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the phrase “relating to” is textually expansive, reaching offenses that are at least “in association with” obstruction-like conduct rather than tracking a narrow common-law definition requiring a pending proceeding. See Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc., 504 U.S. 374, 383 (1992). Accessory-after-the-fact conduct—intentional assistance to hinder apprehension or punishment—fits comfortably within that broad formulation even absent an already-filed case or ongoing investigation, and Congress’s aggravated-felony scheme reflects a practical judgment to treat such serious, law-enforcement-impeding crimes as deportation triggers. Any residual ambiguity does not justify a lenity-based narrowing where Congress has vested interpretive primacy in the Executive for immigration administration, and the Board’s longstanding interpretation is at least reasonable under INS v. Aguirre-Aguirre, 526 U.S. 415, 424 (1999).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) defines an aggravated felony as “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” but the generic meaning of “obstruction of justice” is best understood as interference with the administration of justice in connection with a pending or ongoing investigation or judicial proceeding; Virginia accessory-after-the-fact can be committed without that nexus, so it is not a categorical match. Even if the phrase “relating to” introduces some breadth, any lingering ambiguity in a deportation-triggering provision must be resolved in the noncitizen’s favor given deportation’s severe consequences. Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan instructs that we may not assume Congress meant to trench on a noncitizen’s liberty “beyond that which is required by the narrowest of several possible meanings,” and that principle counsels against expanding § 1101(a)(43)(S) to reach crimes lacking a proceeding nexus. Fair notice and access-to-justice concerns reinforce that aggravated-felony categories should not be stretched to impose mandatory removal based on convictions that do not clearly fit the generic offense.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the phrase “relating to” is textually expansive, reaching crimes that bear a substantial connection to obstruction even if they do not track every element of a narrow generic federal obstruction offense. Reading in a rigid pending-proceeding nexus would sit uneasily with Congress’s use of that broader modifier and with the evident statutory purpose of capturing serious interference with the administration of justice, including intentional hindrance before authorities have initiated formal proceedings. To the extent there is residual ambiguity, the INA assigns interpretive primacy to the Attorney General, and under INS v. Aguirre-Aguirre the Board’s long-standing, reasonable construction merits deference over a lenity-based narrowing. Fong Haw Tan’s caution in deportation cases does not override that delegated interpretive scheme where the text and structure support the broader reading.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the ordinary meaning of “obstruction” is conduct that intentionally impedes the administration of law, not only conduct tied to a formally pending proceeding. Congress’s use of the expansive modifier “relating to” signals a broader sweep than the core federal obstruction statutes and comfortably reaches accessory-after-the-fact offenses that purposefully hinder apprehension or punishment, even before a proceeding is underway. While Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan counsels restraint in construing deportation triggers, that principle cannot override text that Congress wrote, and any lenity-like canon applies only after genuine ambiguity remains. On this reading, the Virginia accessory-after-the-fact offense can qualify as an aggravated felony because it bears a sufficient relationship to obstructive conduct within the statutory phrase.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the breadth of “relating to” indicates Congress intended to reach a range of obstruction-type crimes, not a narrow subset limited to interference with a formally pending proceeding. Historically and as a practical matter, core obstruction-related conduct includes acts designed to impede the administration of justice at its inception (such as assisting an offender to evade apprehension), even if an investigation or proceeding is not yet underway, and adopting petitioner’s categorical nexus requirement would unduly narrow the statute and create workability problems across States’ varied formulations. While petitioner invokes lenity in the removal context, the better reading here is that the text is sufficiently capacious that the tie-breaking canon does not control. The Fourth Circuit’s approach in Ramirez v. Sessions and its application to Virginia accessory-after-the-fact accords with that textual and functional understanding of § 1101(a)(43)(S).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(S) incorporates a term of art—“obstruction of justice”—and in 1996 its established generic meaning in federal law centered on interference with a pending judicial proceeding, as reflected in the core obstruction statute, 18 U.S.C. § 1503. This Court reaffirmed that understanding in United States v. Aguilar, 515 U.S. 593 (1995), which required a nexus to a pending proceeding for § 1503’s omnibus clause; Congress is presumed to legislate against that settled backdrop when it used the phrase in the INA. While the INA adds “relating to,” that phrase cannot erase the essential element that defines the generic offense, and any lingering ambiguity in a deportation-triggering provision is read narrowly under Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6 (1948). Because Virginia accessory-after-the-fact can be committed without a nexus to a pending or ongoing proceeding, it falls outside § 1101(a)(43)(S).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) defines an aggravated felony as “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the most administrable, notice-providing way to apply that category is to hew to the well-settled generic meaning of obstruction—interference with a pending or ongoing investigation or judicial proceeding—rather than expand it to pre-investigative conduct. Reading “relating to” to erase any nexus requirement risks sweeping in a broad range of post-offense conduct (including Virginia accessory-after-the-fact) in a manner that undermines procedural fairness and predictability in plea bargaining and removal consequences. Where Congress has not spoken with clarity in a deportation-triggering provision, our longstanding rule of strict construction requires resolving lingering ambiguity in the noncitizen’s favor. See Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6, 10 (1948) (courts should not assume Congress meant to trench on freedom beyond the narrowest meaning), reinforced by the severe practical consequences of removal.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a conviction qualifies as an INA “aggravated felony” under the category “an offense relating to obstruction of justice” only if the underlying offense requires a nexus to a pending or ongoing investigation or judicial proceeding.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(S) (defining an aggravated felony to include “an offense relating to obstruction of justice”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pugin argues that the phrase “offense relating to obstruction of justice” incorporates the settled, generic meaning of obstruction of justice, which historically and in federal law requires interference with a pending or reasonably foreseeable official proceeding/investigation; therefore a state accessory-after-the-fact offense (especially a misdemeanor form) that can be committed without any proceeding or investigation underway cannot categorically match “obstruction of justice,” and ambiguity should be resolved in the noncitizen’s favor given the severe deportation consequences.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General argues that § 1101(a)(43)(S) covers a broader range of crimes than only those tied to a pending/ongoing proceeding because Congress used the expansive phrase “relating to,” and obstruction-of-justice concepts include efforts to hinder the process of justice even before a proceeding formally begins; thus offenses like accessory after the fact can qualify even without a required nexus to a pending or ongoing investigation or judicial proceeding.
key_precedents: Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6 (1948)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that § 1512(f)(1) still targets interference with an “official proceeding,” so it arguably supports retaining a justice-process nexus and prevents “relating to” from collapsing into generic hindering. But that does not justify adding Petitioner’s categorical requirement that a proceeding be pending or reasonably foreseeable as an element of the INA generic offense; Congress in 1996 used “relating to” alongside a Chapter 73 backdrop that expressly contemplates obstruction conduct occurring before any proceeding is pending, which undercuts the claim that temporality is part of the settled core. Justice Sotomayor is right to warn against untethered breadth in a deportation trigger, yet Fong Haw Tan operates only with grievous ambiguity, and the text-plus-context here supports a narrower limiting principle: the offense must bear a close connection to obstructive interference with the administration of justice (not mere evasion), without imposing an atextual pending/foreseeable proceeding requirement. On that minimal ground, I remain with the Respondent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that “obstruction of justice” is a term of art anchored to interference with an official proceeding and that “relating to” cannot erase that anchor; but the enacted text uses the broader phrase “relating to,” which in ordinary public meaning expands coverage to offenses closely connected to obstruction-type interference even if they do not mirror every element of a generic core. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on 18 U.S.C. § 1512(f)(1) is significant because it shows that, in the relevant period, Congress treated obstruction as reaching conduct without a pending proceeding, undercutting the claim that a pending/foreseeable-proceeding nexus is an indispensable baseline. Justice Sotomayor’s Fong Haw Tan/lenity argument does not justify inserting an atextual categorical limitation absent grievous ambiguity, and the statutory context points toward breadth with limits supplied by “obstruction” itself rather than a hard temporal nexus. I therefore remain persuaded that the respondent’s reading best follows the text as written while still requiring a genuine connection to obstructing the administration of justice, not mere evasion.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that § 1512(f)(1) still presupposes an “official proceeding” as the object of interference, and thus supports retaining a justice-process anchor rather than expanding (S) into generic hindering of law enforcement. But Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett persuasively show that Congress in 1996 used “obstruction” concepts to reach pre-proceeding interference and then, in § 1101(a)(43)(S), added the capacious connector “relating to,” which textually signals coverage beyond a narrow, element-by-element proceeding-nexus definition. Justice Sotomayor’s Fong Haw Tan caution matters in deportation contexts, yet as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, it applies only with grievous ambiguity; here the statutory backdrop and Congress’s choice of phrasing cut against importing an atextual categorical “pending/foreseeable proceeding” requirement. The limiting principle is not “any help to a criminal,” but a close relationship to obstructive interference with the administration of justice, and that is better enforced through a tight understanding of “relating to” than by rewriting the statute to add a universal proceeding nexus.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on § 1512(f)(1) is the strongest pushback, but it still presupposes an “official proceeding” as the object of interference; it relaxes timing, not the core justice-process nexus that gives “obstruction of justice” its term-of-art meaning. Chief Justice Roberts’ and Justice Thomas’ reading lets “relating to” do too much work, effectively converting § 1101(a)(43)(S) into a generalized hindering/accessory category without the limiting principle Congress chose—an expansion with mandatory-removal consequences that we should not infer lightly. Under our generic-offense framework, “relating to” may loosen element-by-element congruence, but it cannot dissolve the very feature that distinguishes obstruction from mere post-crime assistance. Given that residual mismatch, Fong Haw Tan’s caution against enlarging deportation triggers without clear congressional command supports holding the line on the justice-process nexus.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that § 1512(f)(1) still presupposes an “official proceeding,” so it cannot justify untethering § 1101(a)(43)(S) from the justice-process core; that is a real limiting-principle concern for any “relating to” clause. But I agree with Justice Barrett that § 1512(f)(1)’s express rejection of a pending-or-imminent proceeding requirement materially undercuts Petitioner’s effort to constitutionalize a categorical proceeding-nexus as the baseline meaning of “obstruction” in 1996, and the INA’s added words “relating to” further loosen any element-for-element generic match. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Fong Haw Tan matters, but as the Chief Justice notes it operates only with grievous ambiguity; here the text-plus-context gives us enough clarity to reject an atextual categorical limiter while still insisting on a meaningful connection to obstruction-type interference with the administration of justice (not mere evasion). On pragmatic textualist grounds, Respondent’s reading best preserves statutory coherence across the aggravated-felony list without turning (S) into a boundless hindering category.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on 18 U.S.C. § 1512(f)(1) is the most serious textual point for Respondent, but it ultimately reinforces—not weakens—the generic anchor: even where a proceeding “need not be pending,” the statute still makes interference with an “official proceeding” the object, preserving a justice-process nexus rather than authorizing a free-floating “hindering law enforcement” category. Chief Justice Roberts’ concern about lacking an administrable limiting principle if we insist on a proceeding/investigation nexus overlooks that Congress itself supplied the limiter by selecting the term of art “obstruction of justice,” and our generic-offense cases do not allow “relating to” to erase the settled core meaning of the referenced offense. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right that “relating to” broadens coverage, but broadening cannot dissolve the element that distinguishes obstruction from mere accessory-after-the-fact assistance untethered to any contemplated official process. With mandatory-removal consequences in the background, Fong Haw Tan’s caution still counsels against adopting the Board’s expansive construction absent a clearer command than this text provides.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point: “obstruction of justice” carries a traditional justice-process nexus, and we should not let “relating to” dissolve the term of art into generic hindering of law enforcement. But Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on the 1996 Chapter 73 backdrop—particularly § 1512(f)(1)’s express statement that an official proceeding “need not be pending or about to be instituted”—undercuts the claim that a pending-or-foreseeable proceeding is an essential baseline feature of “obstruction” as Congress used that concept when it enacted § 1101(a)(43)(S). Institutionally, importing a categorical pending-proceeding requirement would be an atextual limiter that invites inconsistent results, whereas a limiting principle can be supplied by requiring a close connection to obstruction-type interference with the administration of justice (not mere flight or evasion). Fong Haw Tan’s caution, emphasized by Justice Sotomayor, is important, but I agree with the Chief Justice that it applies only with grievous ambiguity, which I do not find given the enacted phrase “relating to” and the contemporaneous statutory context.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that § 1512(f)(1) still presupposes an “official proceeding” as the object of interference, and thus supports keeping a justice-process nexus as the term-of-art anchor. But § 1101(a)(43)(S) does not incorporate “official proceeding” language; it uses the broader connective “relating to,” and (as Justice Kagan emphasizes) Congress in the same era treated obstruction as reaching pre-proceeding conduct—undercutting the claim that a pending-or-foreseeable proceeding is an essential element of the 1996 public meaning. Justice Sotomayor is right to worry about “relating to” becoming limitless, so the limiting principle must be that the offense bears a close connection to obstruction-type interference with the administration of justice, not mere evasion or generalized hindering. Given that textual breadth and statutory context, I do not see the grievous ambiguity Fong Haw Tan requires to justify adding an atextual categorical proceeding requirement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on § 1512(f)(1) is the strongest point for Respondent, because it confirms Congress knew how to reach obstruction before a proceeding is pending; but that provision still makes an “official proceeding” the object of interference, which preserves—rather than eliminates—the justice-process nexus that gives “obstruction of justice” its term-of-art content. Chief Justice Roberts’ proposed limiting principle (“close connection” to administration of justice) strikes me as too indeterminate under the categorical approach and risks letting “relating to” swallow the anchor term, effectively converting (S) into a general hindering/accessory category Congress did not name. Given the severe aggravated-felony consequences and the mismatch between an accessory statute that can be satisfied without any proceeding/investigation nexus and the generic obstruction core, I do not find the text and context clear enough to expand (S) that far; where the boundary is contested, Fong Haw Tan’s caution remains relevant even if not dispositive. On pragmatic grounds, a proceeding-or-foreseeable-proceeding nexus remains the administrable line that tracks how obstruction differs from mere post-crime assistance.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) defines an aggravated felony to include “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and Congress’s use of “relating to” signals a deliberately broader sweep than the narrow, proceeding-specific elements of any single obstruction statute. A categorical requirement that the offense include a nexus to a pending or ongoing proceeding finds no clear anchor in the text of § 1101(a)(43)(S) and risks importing a limiting element Congress did not adopt, particularly where obstruction concepts can cover efforts to prevent the administration of justice before a proceeding formally begins. While the deportation consequences counsel caution, the rule of lenity applies only to grievous ambiguity, and the statutory language here supports a narrow holding that a pending/ongoing-proceeding nexus is not required. This construction respects Congress’s phrasing while avoiding a disruptive narrowing of an enumerated aggravated-felony category that would undermine uniform administration of immigration law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the ordinary meaning of “relating to” is expansive rather than limiting the category to crimes with a pending-proceeding nexus. Contemporary federal obstruction provisions in Chapter 73 include offenses—such as 18 U.S.C. § 1512—that can be committed without a proceeding already pending, which is strong evidence that “obstruction of justice” was not publicly understood in 1996 to require that element. Reading an atextual pending-proceeding requirement into § 1101(a)(43)(S) would improperly narrow Congress’s chosen language and intrude on the political branches’ immigration judgments. Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan does not justify overriding clear statutory breadth here, because the statute’s wording and structure indicate Congress meant to reach more than obstruction tied to an ongoing proceeding.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and Congress’s use of the expansive phrase “relating to” indicates it did not confine the aggravated-felony category to the precise elements of any single federal obstruction statute requiring a pending or ongoing proceeding. Accessory-after-the-fact and similar crimes that intentionally hinder the administration of justice by preventing apprehension or prosecution comfortably “relat[e] to” obstruction even if a formal proceeding has not yet begun, and a contrary rule would create an easily exploited loophole with substantial practical consequences for immigration enforcement. The rule of lenity in immigration (as discussed in Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan) does not justify rewriting the statutory breadth where the text points the other way. Given the statute’s wording and the law-enforcement interests Congress sought to protect, I would hold that a pending/ongoing-proceeding nexus is not categorically required under § 1101(a)(43)(S).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) must be read against the settled, generic understanding of “obstruction of justice,” which has historically centered on interference with a pending or at least reasonably foreseeable official proceeding or investigation; a state accessory-after-the-fact offense that can be completed with no such nexus does not categorically match that generic core. Although Congress used the broad phrase “relating to,” that cannot erase the essential feature that distinguishes obstruction from mere after-the-fact assistance, especially when the aggravated-felony label triggers mandatory, severe removal consequences. Where the statute’s reach remains uncertain at the margins, this Court applies the immigration rule of lenity and construes lingering ambiguities in favor of the noncitizen. Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6, 10 (1948), counsels that we should not assume Congress meant to impose the harsh consequence of deportation “beyond that which is required by the narrowest of several possible meanings.”

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the phrase “relating to” is an intentionally expansive connector that Congress has used in the aggravated-felony list to sweep more broadly than a tight, element-for-element match. Nothing in the text of (S) adds a limiting modifier like Mellouli’s cross-referenced “defined in section 802 of Title 21,” so statutory context does not “tug” toward importing a categorical pending-proceeding nexus. Reading “obstruction of justice” to include paradigmatic crimes like witness tampering—where federal law expressly dispenses with a pending-proceeding requirement, see 18 U.S.C. § 1512(f)(1)—makes (S) more coherent and workable than a rule that would exclude substantial pre-proceeding interference with the administration of justice. Given that the statutory design and ordinary meaning of “relating to” support the Board’s broader construction, the rule of lenity from Fong Haw Tan does not control absent genuine, grievous ambiguity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) uses a legal term of art—“obstruction of justice”—and the best reading is that Congress incorporated its settled, generic meaning, which historically and in federal usage turns on interference with an existing or at least reasonably foreseeable official proceeding. The government’s reliance on the phrase “relating to” cannot erase the core element that gives the category its meaning; otherwise the provision risks collapsing into any hindrance of law enforcement, untethered to the justice process the term “obstruction of justice” denotes. Nor should we defer to the Board’s interpretation where the statute supplies the relevant meaning and where deference would effectively expand an aggravated-felony ground with severe consequences—an area where this Court has cautioned that ambiguity is not lightly presumed against the noncitizen. Any remaining doubt about the scope of this aggravated-felony label should be resolved narrowly given the “drastic measure” of deportation. See 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(S); Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6 (1948).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and Congress’s use of the capacious phrase “relating to” signals an intent to reach crimes that are associated with obstruction-type conduct even if they do not require a formal, pending proceeding as an element. As a matter of history and federal law, obstruction concepts extend to efforts to thwart the administration of justice at early stages, and requiring a categorical “pending/ongoing proceeding” nexus would be an extra-textual limitation that undermines practical workability and uniform administration under the INA. To the extent there is residual ambiguity, longstanding agency interpretation is entitled to deference under INS v. Aguirre-Aguirre, and the rule of lenity is not a first-resort canon in this context. Fong Haw Tan’s admonition to construe deportation statutes narrowly cannot override the statutory text and structure where Congress has chosen broad language (“relating to”) to define aggravated felonies.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) covers “an offense relating to obstruction of justice,” and the ordinary meaning of “relating to” is expansive, signaling Congress’s intent to reach offenses that bear a close connection to obstruction principles even if they do not require a pending proceeding as an element. Contemporaneous federal law treated certain paradigmatic obstruction crimes as not demanding a temporal nexus—for example, 18 U.S.C. § 1512(f)(1) makes clear that witness tampering can occur even when no official proceeding is pending—undercutting the claim that a pending or ongoing proceeding was part of the generic meaning incorporated in 1996. Given that Congress used a broader “relating to” formulation (rather than defining the aggravated felony as obstruction of justice simpliciter), a categorical requirement of a pending/ongoing proceeding would read a limitation into the text that Congress did not supply. While the rule of lenity recognized in cases like Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan counsels caution in deportation statutes, it does not justify overriding the breadth of the statutory text where the best reading is that a nexus-to-pending-proceeding element is not required.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(43)(S) is an aggravated-felony trigger with exceptionally severe, often mandatory, removal consequences, so we should not read “offense relating to obstruction of justice” to sweep in conduct that lacks the traditional nexus to a pending or at least reasonably foreseeable official proceeding or investigation. Although “relating to” is broad, it cannot erase the core limiting feature of the generic offense as commonly understood when Congress added the provision in 1996, which focuses on willful interference with an investigation or legal process rather than mere post-crime assistance untethered to any proceeding. Given the INA’s reliance on categorical analysis of elements, a state accessory-after-the-fact offense that can be committed without any such nexus does not categorically match obstruction of justice under § 1101(a)(43)(S). Any lingering ambiguity in applying an aggravated-felony label that mandates deportation should be resolved in the noncitizen’s favor under this Court’s longstanding caution in deportation statutes.
